newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO-Russia deal -- an elusive goal.
newsitem.headline: NATO-Russia deal -- an elusive goal.

text.p: NATO's first real negotiating stint with Moscow over a new relationship has underlined the difficulty of creating a post-Cold War security order in Europe while the alliance insists on expanding eastwards.

Diplomats and analysts said a meeting between alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Moscow on Monday had revealed how far apart the two sides were over the issue of alliance enlargement.

Alliance officials said both sides simply used the occasion -- five hours at an official guest house outside Moscow -- to lay out widely differing views of how to address Europe's future security needs with no sign of any common ground.
"It is a long, hard road ahead, but we are reasonably encouraged. There is still everything to play for," said one western ambassador.
NATO intends to name its first new members for two decades at a special summit in Madrid in July. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic currently lead the field.
To sweeten the pill of granting membership to Moscow's former communist satellites, the West has frequently said it wanted to clinch a new relationship with Russia at the same time.
Now NATO officials, stressing enlargement will still go ahead, are admitting the Russia deal may have to wait until later.
"The deal on offer to the Russians is for before, at or after the July summit," said one diplomat. "If it is "after', so be it, we are relaxed. The important thing is we get a good deal in the end."

Independent analysts said they detected a subtle change of emphasis by alliance officials who previously always indicated they expected the deal before July with Russia seeking to make the most of a "done deal".
"It is clear it is going to take a lot more time," said one official.

Analysts say the new realism coincides with the first signs of unease over enlargement emerging in the U.S. foreign-policy establishment which increasingly sees the issue as the major diplomatic test of President Bill Clinton's second term.

Critics fear modernising the armies of new members could divert funds from economic development and actually undermine European stability -- particularly while so many ethnic conflicts remain unresolved.
NATO officials said Monday's meeting was "positive", stressing the fact negotiations had actually started after months of shadow boxing was in itself a major achievement.
"The Russians accepted Solana as a real interlocutor and agreed to meet again. This represents progress though of course we don't want misplaced euphoria about it," another ambassador said.
He added that Primakov was an astute negotiator who was never expected to make any concessions at the first meeting.
"The real question is whether or not he has a mandate from (President Boris) Yeltsin to make concessions at a later date," he told Reuters.
Though no date was set, Primakov indicated he was likely to meet Solana again in mid-February.
Senior aides would, meanwhile, visit NATO's Brussels headquarters to flesh out details of an alliance offer of a permanent consultative mechanism in about two weeks.
"Although the Russians are not fundamentally changing their position, no one expected them to and the atmospherics are good. That is progress," said one official.

NATO officials said they had also succeeded in passing over the message the alliance considered a new relationship with Russia to be a goal within its own right and not simply as a by-product for Moscow's acquiescence to enlargement.
"We want a close, productive relationship with Russia and that stands on its own merit. It is not some sort of consolation prize for enlargement," said one senior official.
Solana presented Primakov with detailed plans for a permanent consultative mechanism and indicated the alliance was prepared to show more flexibility on outstanding arms control issues.
Russia, which favours the new security order taking shape in the orbit of the much-larger Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), presented counter-proposals.

"The real negotiating will take place not on the shape of the consultative forum itself but on what we can then do together without going over the heads of other countries," added the senior official.
